source.title: Evaluating the Impact of SAE-based Language Steering on LLM Performance
source.authors: S. Zwirner; Wentao Hu; Koshiro Aoki; Daisuke Kawahara

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE-derived language features as a steering method to evaluate multilingual task performance. It does not test whether superposition, capacity pressure, polysemanticity, or SAE features as canonical representation units explain model representations.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses polysemanticity and superposition as motivation, but reports no experiment testing those claims. Its own results measure language steering and task performance, not the representation claims in V1–V6. Comparator results for prompting and language-neuron steering are not separately recorded because they do not measure the claim's subject.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained SAE language features as a steering tool and reports only steering performance (language accuracy, BLEU, QA accuracy) against prompting and language neurons. It does not measure superposition, polysemanticity, feature geometry, or SAE feature completeness or canonicity. Superposition and polysemanticity appear only as motivation and post-hoc explanation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAE steering can hurt task performance and output quality in some settings, consistently beats language-neuron steering, and slightly underperforms prompting on translation. On MLQA, steering gives stronger language control than prompting, and combining the two gives the best control and accuracy. They attribute the advantage over neurons to SAE features being less affected by polysemanticity and superposition; this is speculative and untested.
record.recipe_differences: The paper follows Chou et al. (2025)'s SAE language-steering approach, but scores features by differences against all observed languages rather than only English and uses the score as steering strength. It is not a reproduction of the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varied by layer and language; the paper reports later-layer steering was generally more effective, with an exception for Chinese on Llama 3.1 8B. Translation results also varied with steering-strength multipliers.

fits_no_version.finding: Single language-specific SAE decoder directions steer output language in Gemma 2 2B/9B and Llama 3.1 8B (translation accuracy 74–100%). They outperform Kojima language-neuron steering in all 15 settings but give lower BLEU than prompting. On Llama MLQA, steering beats prompting on target-language rate and steering plus prompting is best.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-derived language features steer multilingual output more effectively than individual language neurons, at some cost to output quality.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, Volume 4: Student Research Workshop
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results. The translation analysis selects best-performing features, and the MLQA evaluation uses an LLM judge. Results cover three open-weight models, five languages in translation, and three target languages in QA; the authors also note that pretrained SAE availability limits model coverage and that SAE reconstruction is imperfect.
record.rows_left_out: Layer-wise results in Figures 3–4 and 7–9 and steering-strength plots in Figures 5 and 10–11 are not itemized. The plots report results by layer or strength without tabulated values; the text summarizes the general layer trend and says increasing strength raises language accuracy while BLEU rises only slightly, but no exact values are stated.

untested.parts: No toy models; no test of overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of capacity competition or of dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity sources of polysemanticity.

Pretrained SAEs are used, but there is no test of distributed representation or of SAE recovery of sparse features as a representation claim. SAE steering beating neuron steering is a control-efficacy result, not a representation test.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity. The authors only note in Limitations that SAE reconstruction is imperfect.

missing.what: Language-neuron steering comparator results: accuracy 0–80% and BLEU 0.1–18.02, versus SAE steering. This is relevant to the fits_no_version finding (SAE features versus neurons), not to any version.
Steer+Prompt condition on MLQA (e.g., ES 95% in target language, overall accuracy 0.64).

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly linked to 'none'. They report steering efficacy, not any representation claim. The authors' superposition remark is a post-hoc interpretation, not evidence on V2 or V4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in toy models.
The paper mentions polysemanticity and superposition as a rationale for SAE steering but does not test capacity competition, dedicated dimensions, or shared features.
The paper does not test whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure.

The study uses pretrained SAEs and steers selected features, but does not test whether real-model features are distributed across neurons or establish SAE recovery as evidence for that representation claim.
The paper notes that SAE reconstruction is imperfect and residual loss remains, but does not test feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The paper does not test whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.
